description Write v2 bright lyrics, its Suno lyrics file and run, and commit
sed -i '' 's/the kid'"'"'s name in the Nanit line/the kid'"'"'s name in the monitor line/' songs/2am-crying/LYRICS.md && cat >> songs/2am-crying/LYRICS.md <<'EOF'

---

## v2: bright and innocent

Same chorus, different baby. No parenting jargon, no snark. This baby does not know what a
clock is, only that when you say a number in the dark, you come. Crying isn't sadness; it's
the one word it has that works at night. Musically brighter: major key, bells, toy piano,
bubblegum Eurodance, a music-box intro. The escalation is joy instead of exhaustion:
*I'm crying → you came → we're dancing → the sun came too → napping.*

**[Intro]** *(music box, soft; a small yawn; the beat fades in)*
> I woke up. It's dark. Hello?
> *(untz. untz. untz. untz.)*

**[Verse 1]**
> The room is dark, the fan goes round, the ocean sound is on.
> I opened up my eyes to check on you, and you were gone.
> I don't know what a clock is, but you say numbers in the night,
> And every number means you're coming, and you bring the light.
> I learned to stand today! I need to show you right away.
> I'm not sad. I'm just loud. Loud is the only word I can say.
> The dark is big and I am small, and that's okay, because
> I know a way to find you. I'll do it now. Here it goes:

**[Chorus]**
> It's 2am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 3am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 4am and you came!
> It's 11am and I'm napping

**[Post-Chorus]**
> *(untz untz untz untz) (shh shh, I'm here)*
> *(untz untz untz untz) (shh shh, I'm here)*

**[Verse 2]**
> You carry me along the hall like we are going somewhere.
> We're not. We're going down the hall. I love it. I don't care.
> You bounce, I bounce, the floor goes boom, the boom goes in my feet.
> I think you made this song for me. I think this is the beat.
> You hum the song that's not a song. I know it. It's my favorite.
> I pointed at the moon. You looked! I did that. I'm the bravest.
> Your face is close and tired and it is my favorite face.
> I'd like to stay like this forever. Is forever a place?

**[Pre-Chorus]**
> You put me down. You tiptoe out. I count to one. And then
> I know a way to find you. Here it goes again:

**[Chorus]**
> It's 2am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 3am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 4am and we're dancing!
> It's 11am and I'm napping

**[Bridge]** *(music box, half-time, sunlight)*
> It's 11am and I'm napping.
> I close my eyes and the room goes somewhere, and I go with it.
> I dream about the stairs. I dream the word for "dog." I dream your face.
> And when I wake up, you're still here. You're always here.
> That's my favorite trick. You do it every time.
> And tonight, when it gets dark, I'll check again:

**[Final Chorus]**
> It's 2am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 3am and I'm crying *(I'm crying)*
> It's 4am and we're dancing!
> It's 5am and the sun came too!
> It's 11am and I'm napping

**[Outro]** *(soft; the beat stops; one small voice)*
> Good morning. You're here.
> *(untz.)*

### What v2 keeps from the research

- "I learned to stand today, I need to show you": babies really do practice new motor
  skills at night, and it's one of the better-supported causes of wakings.
- "I pointed at the moon. You looked!": pointing to share attention arrives around 12
  months and is the first joint-attention milestone.
- "I dream about the stairs": naps consolidate what was learned that day.
- "You bounce, I bounce, the floor goes boom": the hallway bounce is the tempo.

### Which to run

Run both. v1 is the funnier video; v2 is the one that could make a grandparent cry. If
only one, v2 is the safer song and v1 the safer video.
EOF

## Run D: v2 bright and innocent (lyrics file `suno_lyrics_v2_bright.txt`)

```
~/.local/bin/suno generate \
  --title "2AM (And I'm Crying) [bright]" \
  --model v5.5 \
  --vocal female \
  --tags "bubblegum eurodance, 128 bpm, four-on-the-floor, major key, bright bell synths, toy piano, music box intro, sidechained warm pads, offbeat hats, sweet clear childlike female vocal, innocent, euphoric but gentle drop, half-time music box bridge, sunrise, hopeful, clean mix" \
  --exclude "dark, aggressive, distorted, acoustic ballad, slow tempo, rock guitar, metal, lo-fi, mumbled vocals, autotune artifacts" \
  --style-influence 70 --weirdness 25 \
  --lyrics-file /Users/jalex/projects/clawdpop/songs/2am-crying/suno_lyrics_v2_bright.txt \
  --wait --download /Users/jalex/projects/clawdpop/songs/2am-crying/audio/runD
```

A second v2 pass worth one run: `--tags "happy hardcore lite, 150 bpm, bouncy, bright piano
stabs, bells, sweet female vocal, kids-TV energy, four-on-the-floor"`. Faster tempo makes the
"you came!" lines land like a cheer.
EOF

**[Outro]** *(soft; the beat stops; one small voice)*
> Good morning. The fan is still on.
> *(untz.)*

### What v2 keeps from the research

- "I learned to stand today": babies practice new motor skills at night; it's one of the
  better-supported causes of wakings.
- "I drop it off the side. It's gone! ...It's on the ground": the 9-to-14-month dropping
  phase is the baby running gravity and object-permanence experiments.
- "I dream about the stairs": naps consolidate what was learned that day.
- "My hands go slow. My eyes go slow": the milk-drunk state is real and much loved.

### Which to run

Run both. v1 is the funnier video; v2 is the one that could make a grandparent cry. If
only one, v2 is the safer song and v1 the safer video.

## v3: the day (lead version)

Inspiration: the "Imma Be" day-in-my-life selfie trend. The baby is filming its own day on
a phone, front camera, one clip per timestamp, caption in the corner. Every line is

the verses are the same form at double speed filling in the rest of the day, and the day
is a loop (the last line is the first line). Jokes come from the rhythm: cry, cry, cry,
nap; cry, poop, poop again.

> *(untz. untz. untz. untz.)*

> It's 11am and I'm napping *(nap-nap-napping)*
> It's 12pm and I'm crying
> It's 1pm and I'm pooping
> It's 2pm and I'm pooping again

**[Verse 2: afternoon to night, double-time]**
> It's 3pm and I'm napping. It's 4pm and I'm drinking.
> It's 5pm and I'm crying. It's 5:30 and I'm crying at the fan.
> It's 6pm and I'm eating. It's 6:05 and the floor is eating.

> It's 10:58 and I'm heavy.
> It's 11am and I'm napping.

**[Final Chorus]** *(biggest; the whole day in one pass)*

> It's 4am and I'm crying
> It's 11am and I'm napping
> It's 12pm and I'm crying
> It's 1pm and I'm pooping
> It's 2pm and I'm pooping again
> It's 3pm and I'm napping
> It's 7pm and I'm splashing
> It's 8pm and I'm sleeping
> It's 1am and I'm...

**[Outro]** *(spoken, same as the intro; the loop closes)*
> Hi. It's me. Here's my day.
> *(click)*

### Notes

- The user's seven lines are the chorus, verbatim. Everything else is the same form.
- The times follow a real two-nap day: up before 6, nap around 11, nap around 3, bath at 7,
  down by 8. The night section ends in "sleeping" lines that get sleepier, then the
  1am ellipsis, then 2am and the loop.
- "You're sleeping" at 10pm is the one line where the camera turns around.
- The bottle verse from v2 is compressed into the bridge: drinking → warm → heavy → napping.
- For a 60-second TikTok cut: intro, chorus, verse 2 from "8pm", outro.


Second pass if the first is too rap: swap the tags to "bubblegum eurodance, 128 bpm, bright
bells, sweet childlike female vocal, stutter edits, deadpan timestamps" (the v2 sound on the
v3 words).

Listen for: every timestamp intelligible; the one-bar silence after "1am and I'm..."; the
double-time verses actually at double density, not stretched to one line per bar.

git mv songs/2am-crying/TREATMENT.md songs/2am-crying/TREATMENT-v1-monitor.md && cat > songs/2am-crying/TREATMENT.md <<'EOF'
# Treatment v3: the baby's selfie video

Supersedes `TREATMENT-v1-monitor.md` (the nursery-camera concept; still a good source for
the night clips and the baby character). Lyrics: `LYRICS.md` → "v3: the day", and
`suno_lyrics_v3_day.txt`.

## Concept

The baby is filming a day-in-my-life video on a phone, front camera, in the style of the
"Imma Be" selfie trend: one clip per timestamp, a caption in the corner that reads exactly
what the lyric says, hard cuts on the beat, and the day looping back to 2am at the end.
Every line of the song is "It's [time] and I'm [doing]", so every line is one clip and the
caption is the lyric. The clock is still the escalating number, but now it lives in the
phone's status bar and in the caption.

Tone: the baby is sincere. It is not performing misery; it is documenting. The phone is
held badly (too close, tilted, thumb on the lens once), which is where the charm comes from.

## Formats

- Primary: vertical 1080x1920 (9:16), the trend's native shape. 60 fps final, 30 fps drafts.
- Secondary: 1920x1080 (16:9) with the vertical phone frame centered on a soft nursery
  backdrop (the room out of focus, time-of-day lighting), for YouTube. Same scenes, one
  layout switch.

## Style bible

- **Look.** A phone front camera: slight wide-angle stretch at the edges, mild over-
  saturation by day, grain and a hard flash at night (the flash lights the baby's face and
  nothing else). Not the IR greyscale of v1, except as a joke for the 7:45pm "sleeping" clip,
  where the parents' monitor view is cut in.
- **Caption.** The trend style: lowercase, heavy grotesque (Archivo Black / Inter 900),
  white with a black outline or on a rounded black pill, upper third of the frame. The
  caption is the lyric line, revealed word by word in sync, and stays until the cut. Times
  are digits ("it's 2am and i'm crying").
- **Status bar.** A thin phone status bar at the top: the clock (which is the escalation
  number), battery draining across the day and charging during naps, a red record dot
  with a running timer.
- **Baby.** The same procedural character as v1: round head, two dot eyes, a few hairs,
  stubby arms; sleep sack at night, onesie by day. One arm always extends toward the bottom
  corner of the frame, holding the phone (we see the upper arm and the elbow, not the phone).
  Expressions are tiny: eyes open/closed/half, mouth a line, an O, or a small smile.
- **Time of day.** Background colour temperature and brightness follow the clock: deep blue
  night, grey-blue 5am, warm 7am, white noon, gold 6pm, blue again at 8pm. A tiny sun/moon
  arc in the backdrop of the 16:9 layout.
- **Motion.** Cuts on downbeats. In the double-time verses, two cuts per bar. The phone
  shakes with the kick, slightly. Slams on "pooping again". No cute wobble beyond the
  selfie handshake.
- **Bans.** No photos, no real faces, no emoji-style faces, no diaper-contents humour.
  "Pooping" is a face and a caption, nothing else.

## Clips

Each clip is anchored to its lyric line by content. Duration is whatever the line's words
cover, snapped to the beat grid.

| line | clip |
|---|---|
| intro "Hi. It's me." | Phone wakes; the baby's face too close, then pulls back; a wave; record dot starts. |
| 2am crying | Dark crib, flash on, mouth an O, eyes squeezed; the caption's "crying" slams. |
| 3am crying | Same framing, phone tilted 15°, a parent silhouette appearing in the doorway behind. |
| 4am crying | Same framing, the parent silhouette now sitting on the floor next to the crib. |
| 11am napping | Hard cut to bright daylight, eyes closed, the phone slowly tipping over to the ceiling fan. |
| 12pm crying | High chair, daylight, a spoon mid-air. |
| 1pm pooping | Concentration face. Caption only. Hold absolutely still. |
| 2pm pooping again | Identical frame to 1pm; the caption gets "again" slammed on in red. |
| 5am quiet | Nearly black; just the record dot and two open eyes. |
| 5:45 up | Flash; the baby standing, grinning; the parents' alarm clock visible behind: 5:45. |
| 6am standing / 6:15 still standing | Same frame twice, the second with a timer overlay. |
| 7am drinking / 7:30 wearing it | Bottle with both hands, eyes half closed; then a milk-stained onesie, proud. |
| 8am eating / 8:05 throwing it | High chair; then food arcing past the lens, a splat on the glass. |
| 9am reading / 9:01 eating it | Board book held up; then the book's corner in the mouth. |
| 10am pointing / 10:30 pointing at the fan | Finger into the lens; then camera whips up to the ceiling fan. |
| 10:45 fighting it | Eyes closing and snapping open, twice, on the beat. |
| 3pm napping | Daylight nap in a car seat or stroller, head at an angle. |
| 4pm drinking | Bottle, golden light. |
| 5pm crying / 5:30 crying at the fan | Witching hour; then the fan again, accusingly. |
| 6pm eating / 6:05 the floor is eating | High chair; then camera tilts down: food on the floor, caption deadpan. |
| 7pm splashing | Bath; water droplets on the lens; the caption drips. |
| 7:15 naked and running | Motion blur, towel cape, the frame shaking, laughter. |
| 7:30 reading / 7:45 "sleeping" | Book in the crib; then dark room, eyes wide open, caption with quotation marks; a one-second cut-in of the v1 IR monitor view. |
| 8pm, 9pm sleeping | Dark, eyes closed, the phone drifting. |
| 10pm you're sleeping | Camera flips to the rear: a parent asleep in the chair, mouth open. The only rear-camera shot. |
| 11pm we're sleeping / 12am sleeping | Darker, slower, the record timer the only motion. |
| 1am and I'm... | Black. Record dot. One bar of silence. Eyes open. |
| bridge 10:50 → 11am | The one long take: bottle, eyes heavy, the phone tilting degree by degree until it lies flat looking at the ceiling fan; the fan's blades slow with the half-time. |
| final chorus | The day as a filling grid of all the clips, 3 wide, each tile lighting on its line, until the 1am tile goes black. |
| outro "Hi. It's me." | The intro clip again, frame-exact, so the video loops. |

## Technical notes

Same engine contract as before: deterministic frames, `data/lyrics.json` word timings,
`data/audio.json` beat grid and sections. One scene module per clip type (crib-night,
high-chair, bath, standing, nap, pooping-face, fan, rear-camera, grid), parameterised by
time-of-day and caption, instead of one module per lyric line. The caption component and
the status bar are shared. A `layout` switch selects 9:16 or 16:9.
EOF

Direction change for the 2am-crying video: the concept has pivoted. Read /Users/jalex/projects/clawdpop/songs/2am-crying/TREATMENT.md again (it is now "Treatment v3: the baby's selfie video"; the old nursery-camera concept moved to TREATMENT-v1-monitor.md) and the new lyrics, "v3: the day", at the bottom of songs/2am-crying/LYRICS.md plus songs/2am-crying/suno_lyrics_v3_day.txt.

What changes:

  • Lyrics: every line is now "It's [time] and I'm [doing]". Chorus is 7 lines; two double-time verses of 8 lines each (two short clauses per line, so two cuts per bar); a half-time bridge; an 11-line final chorus; spoken intro/outro that are identical so the video loops. Regenerate the mock timing from this lyric sheet (chorus ~8 bars, double-time verses 8 bars each, bridge 8 bars, final chorus 12 bars, intro/outro 2 bars each; adjust so boundaries sit on bar lines).
  • Format: primary output is vertical 1080x1920 (9:16); 16:9 is a secondary layout with the phone frame centered on a soft nursery backdrop. Add a layout switch; drafts at 540x960.
  • Look: a phone front camera (selfie), not IR greyscale. Caption = the lyric line in heavy lowercase grotesque, revealed word by word, upper third. A phone status bar with the clock (the escalating number), battery, record dot + timer.
  • Structure: one clip per lyric line, hard cut on the downbeat; scene modules are per clip TYPE (crib-night, high-chair, bath, standing, nap, pooping-face, fan, rear-camera, grid), parameterised by time-of-day colour temperature and the caption, rather than one module per lyric line. Final chorus is a 3-wide grid of the day's clips filling in; outro repeats the intro frame-exactly.

The fact sheet is written: /Users/jalex/projects/clawdpop/songs/baby-facts/FACTS.md — 482 lines, ~11,900 words, 354 flagged facts, 30 hooks, 47 URLs. The only unflagged bullets are the closing "could not verify" list, by design.

Summary of the most lyrically useful findings

  1. The best source turned out to be the episodes themselves: Netflix posted five Part 1 episodes on YouTube, so Love, Crawling, First Words, Sleep and First Steps are documented from the actual audio — exact numbers, quotes and family names (Willow, Pascoe, Dakota, Eric, Nelson, Mateo, twins Kiki/Yaya and Eloisa/Augusto).
  2. Lampl (Ep 3) is the richest vein: a baby measured 62.7 cm, then 64.5 cm the next day ("I'm really terrible at this"); 59.8, 59.8, 59.8, 60.8 cm; growth charts are "connect-the-dots" from 882 children; the 1992 Science paper (31 infants: 0.5–2.5 cm bursts, 2–63 days of stasis, 90–95% of infancy growth-free) made the NYT front page and got her mocked at a conference.
  3. Feldman (Ep 1): 80 couples, fathers' oxytocin "identical" to mothers'; 48 gay couples, primary-caregiving dads' amygdalae light up like mothers'; dad's response otherwise "about a quarter"; "Fatherhood is biological. It's as deep as motherhood." Tronick's professor told him "This emotion stuff is not what you want to be doing."
  4. Saffran (Ep 4): "pabeecoo," 2 minutes, 45 repetitions; her mother's aphasic patient who kept only the noun "shopping center." Jarvis: ex-dancer, "three birds and five mammals" are vocal learners, SRGAP2 extra copy.
  5. Sleep (Ep 5): Wallisch's 6 million app events from ~1,000 babies (1.5M sleeps, 2.5M feeds, 1.5M diapers) — explicitly unpublished; Blumberg's twitch-as-sonar-ping and "we study the things we're bad at"; Spencer's "I'm a lark" and spindles.
  6. First Steps (Ep 6): Dominici's two newborn muscle patterns plus two toddler ones, shared with rat, cat, macaque and guineafowl; Cowgill's 130 lb of gear through 15 museums, 600 children's bones back to 250,000 years, and Reviewer 2's "Children's bones don't respond to exercise"; Walle's 374 words in five minutes and the finding that walkers and crawlers hear the same number of words.
  7. Adolph: 2,368 steps and 17 falls per hour (the 701 m / 7.7 football fields is per hour; ~14,000 steps and ~46 fields per day are extrapolations); "crawling isn't mandatory"; Grant crawled straight over the 90-degree drop.
  8. Killer replication jokes: ManyBabies 4 (567 infants, 37 labs) found 49.3% helper preference for Hamlin's puppet show; Wonder Weeks tested on 4 infants by a PhD student, Plooij lost his job in Jan 1998; Mozart effect was 36 college students for ~10 minutes while Georgia spent $105k on CDs; Baby Einstein refunds $15.99 per DVD; 106 newborns imitated nothing.
  9. Solid numeric gems: French cries rise, German cries fall (1,254 cries); only 43% of 6-month-olds sleep 8 hours; half of newborn sleep is REM; colostrum is three teaspoons on day one; milk leukocytes jump to 94% during infection; 1.49 million Holsteins favor heifers; 22 of 30 newborns pick the unwashed breast; newborn focus at 19 cm.
  10. Corrections to the brief: Feldman's 2014 paper had 48 gay fathers, not 48 couples (the show says couples); newborn sleep is a meta-analytic 14.6 h, not 16–18; teething tops out at 37.8 °C; "300 bones" and "1 million synapses/second" have no primary source.

What I could not verify

  • Part 2 rosters are incomplete: Ep 8 "Movement" has no identifiable scientists; Ep 9 "Senses" has only Mennella (inferred) and no touch/vision names; the third scientists in Eps 11 and 12 are unknown. IMDb credits were blocked (403) and no press release names them. Confirmed Part 2: Hespos, Kang Lee, Saxe (Ep 7, Saxe's placement probable); Reddy, Hamlin, Malinda Carpenter (Ep 10); Gartstein, Rochat (Ep 11); Warneken, Schulz (Ep 12).
  • Not in the series at all (per every accessible source): Kuhl, Dominguez-Bello, Charles Nelson, Spelke, Fei Xu, Tomasello, Fessler, Kidd.
  • On-air glosses to avoid singing as fact: Georgieff's "shift world IQ by ten points," Feldman's "forever" and "a quarter," Barbu-Roth's head as "one third of body weight."
  • The shared WebSearch budget ran out midway (three parallel researchers plus my own searches), so the back half relied on direct fetches of known URLs, NCBI E-utilities and YouTube subtitles; the Rifkin-Graboi, Fenton/Wallisch and Spencer-infant results are described on air but not matched to published papers.

10	
11	- Produced by Nutopia for Netflix; executive producer Jane Root (Nutopia CEO); series producer / EP Sara Brailsford. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babies_(American_TV_series) **[solid]**

15	- Part 1 sat in Netflix's Top 10 for several weeks (Northwestern release); WSU says it "rose to number seven." https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2020/02/netflix-babies-docu-series-features-northwestern-psychology-professor-susan-hespos **[solid]**

31	## 1. Episode by episode
32	
33	### Ep 1 "Love" (Part 1)
34	Netflix: "The biology of bonding unravels to reveal how caregiving, social interaction and stress can physically change both parent and newborn."
35	
36	- **Ruth Feldman** (IDC Herzliya, now Reichman University, Israel; joint appointment Yale Child Study Center). Daughter Estie was placed on her chest when Feldman was 22: "at that moment I felt what it means to love." **[solid, transcript]**
37	- In 2001 she began "the first study to test the role of oxytocin in parent/infant bonding": "about 80 mothers," sampled through pregnancy and the first month; oxytocin rises in pregnancy, stays high, and touch raises it in mother and baby alike. **[solid]**
38	- Next: "80 couples," saliva sampled in the first months; "Mothers' and fathers' level of oxytocin were identical." Gordon, Zagoory-Sharon, Leckman and Feldman 2010, *Biological Psychiatry* 68:377 (160 first-time parents at 6 weeks and 6 months). https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/08/100820101207.htm **[solid]**
39	- Mothers' oxytocin tracks affectionate touch and gaze; fathers' tracks stimulatory play (same paper). **[solid]**
40	- On air: "The more you do with a baby... and really lift your sleeves, and take care of the child... the more your oxytocin system will activate. Fatherhood is biological. It's as deep as motherhood." **[solid, transcript]**
41	- On air: the birth oxytocin surge "activates a very primitive structure. The amygdala... once the mother's amygdala is open, it stays like this forever"; dad's response is "about a quarter of what you see in mom's." **[pop: on-air gloss]**
42	- "In 2010 we recruited... 48 gay couples" raising surrogacy-born babies from day one: primary-caregiving fathers "had amygdala activation just like mothers." **[solid, transcript]**
43	- The paper: Abraham et al. 2014, *PNAS* 111:9792 — 89 parents (20 primary-care mothers, 21 secondary-care fathers, 48 primary-care gay fathers); gay fathers showed mother-like amygdala plus father-like superior-temporal-sulcus activity; amygdala–STS connectivity scaled with hours of childcare (r = 0.33). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4103311/ **[solid]**
44	- Closing line: "It doesn't really matter whether you are the biological parent or a committed caregiving parent. It's a choice. It's a choice to be a parent to that infant." **[solid, transcript]**
45	- **Ed Tronick** (UMass Boston; Harvard Medical School). Arrived at Harvard psychology in 1968, when "everyone was doing hard science"; a professor put an arm round him: "This emotion stuff is not what you want to be doing." **[solid, transcript]**
46	- Still-face: mothers of 3-, 4- and 5-month-olds "stop reacting to the baby for about two minutes"; babies smile, bid, eventually cry, then bring hands to mouth to self-comfort. Tronick, Als, Adamson, Wise and Brazelton 1978, *J Am Acad Child Psychiatry* 17:1 (PMID 632477). **[solid]**
47	- New version adds salivary cortisol: babies with "positive experience with their parents" are less stressed during the still face. Study specifics are not cited on air. **[solid paradigm; result described, not cited]**
48	- Tronick's parenting line: "Trust your baby to tell you what it is that he or she needs and trust your own instincts... That's how the two of you fall in love with one another." **[solid, transcript]**
49	- **Anne Rifkin-Graboi** (National Institute of Education, NTU Singapore), with imaging colleague **Anqi Qiu**: GUSTO cohort (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes). Babies scanned in the first weeks and again at 6 months; babies fed to sleep for the scan. **[solid, transcript]**
50	- "We had 20 babies" rated for maternal responsiveness with a card-sort at 6 months; less responsive caregiving went with "a bit bigger" hippocampi, read as babies "having to manage their own stress." "To my knowledge, that was the first time a group had seen this." **[contested: n = 20, counterintuitive direction, primary paper not located]**
51	- Family beats: Willow's birth opens the series; Josh at Eric's vaccination: "I don't know who is going to suffer more. Him or me." **[solid, transcript]**
52	
53	### Ep 2 "First Food"
54	Netflix: "...how breast milk, iron and microbes can enrich, nourish and protect offspring." (Not on YouTube; roster from the Notre Dame episode summary, Netflix media page, UCSF Lynch Lab page and goodto.com.)
55	
56	- **Katie Hinde** (Arizona State University; comparative lactation). Rhesus mothers of sons make richer, more energy-dense milk; daughters get more volume and a higher calcium:phosphorus ratio. Hinde 2009, *Am J Hum Biol* 21:512 (114 mothers; total milk energy equal); Hinde et al. 2013, *Am J Phys Anthropol* "Daughter dearest." https://doi.org/10.1002/ajhb.20917 **[solid]**
57	- Dairy cows favor daughters: 2.39 million lactation records from 1.49 million Holsteins show ~1.3% more milk (~445 kg over two lactations) after a heifer calf. Hinde, Carpenter, Clay and Bradford 2014, *PLoS ONE* 9:e86169. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0086169 **[solid]**
58	- Milk cortisol predicts temperament: in 108 macaque pairs, higher milk glucocorticoids went with more nervous, less confident, faster-gaining infants. Hinde et al. 2015, *Behav Ecol*. **[solid]**
59	- Hinde on air (per summaries): "an individual mom makes individualized milk for an individual baby"; daily experiences leave "signatures" in milk; the best substitute is formula built from human-milk science, not cow's milk. https://sites.nd.edu/emily-clarke/2019/12/06/chapter-9/ **[solid, secondary]**
60	- Supporting lit for "milk responds to illness": leukocytes are 13–70% of cells in colostrum, 0–2% in mature milk, and surge to as high as 94% during infant or maternal infection (21 dyads). Hassiotou et al. 2013, *Clin Transl Immunol* 2:e3. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25505951/ **[solid, small n]**
61	- **Michael Georgieff** (University of Minnesota, Institute of Child Development; neonatologist). Many babies are short of iron, zinc and copper; babies are born with about four months of iron. **[solid, secondary]**
62	- Iron-sufficient newborns' ERPs distinguish mother's voice from a stranger's; iron-deficient newborns' do not. Siddappa et al. 2004, *Pediatr Res* 55:1034 (32 newborns of diabetic mothers; cord ferritin ≤34 µg/L = brain-iron deficient). **[solid]**
63	- Georgieff's on-air claim: eliminating micronutrient deficiencies worldwide would "shift the world's IQ positively by ten points." **[pop]**
64	- **Susan Lynch** (UCSF). "It's really important for babies to ingest microbes early in life"; babies living with dogs, and to a lesser extent cats, are better protected from asthma and allergy. https://lynchlab.ucsf.edu/node/701 **[solid]**
65	- Dust from dog-owning homes restructures the mouse gut microbiome (Lactobacillus johnsonii) and blunts allergic airway disease. Fujimura et al. 2014, *PNAS* 111:805. **[solid]**
66	- One-month-old stool microbiota fall into three states; the riskiest (NGM3: low Bifidobacterium, Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium, more Candida) predicts multisensitized atopy at 2 and asthma at 4. Fujimura et al. 2016, *Nat Med* 22:1187 (298 samples, median age 35 days). **[solid]**
67	- Also in the episode (goodto.com): a mother's pregnancy diet shapes the baby's food preferences because taste and memory form before birth (see Mennella, Senses theme). **[solid]**
68	- Mothers interviewed: a British mother who loves breastfeeding and a Connecticut mother of twins who stopped for low supply (Notre Dame summary). **[secondary]**

73	- **Marianne Barbu-Roth** (CNRS / Université de Paris). "I started to be a nuclear physicist... studying the movement of electrons and atoms"; a newborn is "an astronaut coming back from the moon... now stuck with the gravity." **[solid, transcript]**

75	- Optic flow: moving black dots projected beneath a suspended newborn make it move "literally swimming. Swimming in the air." Barbu-Roth et al. 2009, *Child Development* 80:8 — 48 three-day-olds; more air-steps to forward-translating flow than to rotating or static patterns. **[solid]**
76	- On air: "this crawling pattern that a lot of people believe was just a reflex is not a reflex." A newborn's head is "one third of the weight of the body." **[solid finding; head figure is pop]**
77	- The "Crawlerskate" (published as the Crawliskate): a mini-skateboard under the trunk; first baby tested 2016 after "one or two years" of building; two-day-olds "even crossed the mattress once or two or three times." Forma et al. 2019, *Child Development*. **[solid]**
78	- "We believe now that we are born moving arms and legs as quadrupeds... We are still quadrupeds inside us, in the nervous system." Her metaphor: "the engine is sleeping and waiting for the bodywork to be ready." **[interpretation]**
79	- **Michelle Lampl** (Emory, Center for the Study of Human Health; MD-PhD anthropologist). 1979: her neighbor's baby measured 62.7 cm one day and 64.5 cm the next, then 64.5 for days: "I'm really terrible at this... that's way too much." **[solid, transcript]**
80	- Growth charts are "connect-the-dots" from 882 children measured at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 weeks and then monthly to one year. **[solid, transcript]**

82	- 19 February 1986: a baby measured 59.8, 59.8, 59.8 and then 60.8 cm — one centimetre in one day. **[solid, transcript]**

84	- The paper: Lampl, Veldhuis and Johnson 1992, *Science* 258:801 — 31 infants (10 weekly, 18 semiweekly, 3 daily) over 21 months; saltations 0.5–2.5 cm; stasis 2–63 days; "90 to 95 percent of normal development during infancy is growth-free." https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1439787/ **[solid, but critics attribute part to measurement error (Science 1995 exchange) — contested]**
85	- Growth days coincided with "changes in their sleeping behavior, tantrums, and times of insatiable hunger." **[solid, transcript]**
86	- Follow-up: length spurts follow sleep bursts within 48 hours; odds of a spurt rise a median 43% per extra sleep episode and 20% per extra hour (23 infants, 5,798 diary days). Lampl and Johnson 2011, *Sleep* 34:641. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079944 **[solid, small n]**

101	### Ep 4 "First Words"
102	Netflix: "Experts examine the rhythm and flow of language and explore how babies break down linguistic beats before they know how to speak."
103	
104	- **Kathy Hirsh-Pasek** (Temple University Infant Language Lab; Brookings). Was "headed toward being a musician"; her aha moment was a three-year-old at a pool complaining about her brother's ballgame "with the sophisticated grammar and language skills of an adult." **[solid, transcript]**
105	- Experiment: a Cinderella passage ("...because she had this mean, mean, mean stepmother") with pauses placed either at clause boundaries or mid-clause, played from left and right speakers; babies "overwhelmingly looked more quickly" and stayed longer on the natural version. **[solid, transcript]**
106	- The paper: Hirsh-Pasek et al. 1987, *Cognition* 26:269, "Clauses are perceptual units for young infants" (7–10-month-olds). **[solid]**
107	- "40 years ago... there was nobody, literally no one in the world, who I could find who was doing music and language together." **[solid, transcript]**
108	- "At just two days of age, we already know that babies recognize classes of language... English and some of the other Germanic languages kinda sound alike." (Newborn rhythm-class discrimination: Nazzi, Bertoncini and Mehler 1998, *JEP:HPP* 24:756; Mehler et al. 1988, *Cognition* 29:143.) **[solid]**
109	- Fetuses hear language "against the backdrop of 'bu-bum, bu-bum,' for the heart, and the swishing sound of the amniotic fluid." **[solid, transcript]**
110	- "At the end of the first year, these babies have kinda cracked the code of what the units of language are. And the next big job is actually finding the words." **[solid, transcript]**
111	- **Jenny Saffran** (University of Wisconsin–Madison Infant Learning Lab). Origin story: her mother studied brain damage; a patient lost every noun except "shopping center" — "The shopping center went to the shopping center to buy the shopping center." **[solid, transcript]**
112	- Made-up language with words like "pabeecoo" and "golatoo," synthesized in a random stream; babies listen "for two minutes" and hear each word "a lot, like 45 times." **[solid, transcript]**
113	- Test: a side light blinks and plays either a word or a non-word for as long as the baby looks; babies "will actually be bored of the words... and they'll turn their heads to listen longer to the sounds that were not words." **[solid, transcript]**
114	- The paper: Saffran, Aslin and Newport 1996, *Science* 274:1926 — 8-month-olds segment words using transitional probabilities of 1.0 within words vs 0.33 across. https://psych.wisc.edu/news/saffrans-infant-learning-lab-featured-on-netflix-docuseries-babies/ **[solid]**
115	- Word meaning by elimination: "doggie" with a stick and a bone one day, a ball and a shoe the next; only the dog is constant. "That is statistical learning as well." **[solid, transcript]**
116	- "By the end of the first year of life they understand somewhere between 10 and 50 words on average... most of them are not saying any words yet." **[solid, transcript]**
117	- Bilingual babies must learn "the statistics not just of one language, but of two" and sort the "two soups" by "musical properties" — rhythm and pitch (cf. Byers-Heinlein, Burns and Werker 2010, *Psychol Sci* 21:343). "It's vastly easier for babies than for older children and adults." **[solid]**
118	- **Erich Jarvis** (Rockefeller University; HHMI). "I was once a dancer... I was dancing six hours a day"; at 18 in 1988, at his senior concert, he chose science "and I never turned back." **[solid, transcript]**
119	- Vocal learners across tens of thousands of vertebrate species: "Three birds and five mammals. That's the hummingbirds, the parrots, songbirds, elephants, bats, dolphins, seals, and human." Jarvis 2019, *Science* 366:50. **[solid]**
120	- Began in 1989 imaging singing birds' brains; "eight years later, an accidental discovery": hopping and wing-flapping lit up regions right next to the song nuclei. Feenders et al. 2008, *PLoS ONE* 3:e1768, the "motor theory of vocal learning origin." **[solid]**

127	Netflix: "Researchers delve into sleep, a dynamic time for babies, with studies on twitching, apps and naps."

129	- **Andre Fenton** (NYU Center for Neural Science). "Getting your baby to sleep through the night turns out to be a universal human challenge." Became a sleep researcher because "all hell broke loose" when he couldn't get his daughter to sleep. **[solid, transcript]**
130	- On air: "A newborn baby is spending 16 hours a day sleeping." (Meta-analytic mean is 14.6 h at 0–2 months; see Sleep theme.) **[contested figure]**
131	- Founded the NYU Baby Sleep Study with baby-tracking app developers; visiting families, he found parents log to the minute, error "no more than five minutes." **[solid, transcript]**
132	- **Pascal Wallisch** (NYU): "about 1,000 babies... six million events made up out of about 1.5 million sleep events, 2.5 million eating events, and 1.5 million diaper change events." **[solid, transcript]**
133	- At one month eating and sleeping are random; "within about four months an initial cycle is emerging"; at eight months "a hint of a pattern"; "within a year, this clear pattern emerges. Babies are sleeping through the night." **[unverified: "we are not comfortable to publish this yet"]**
134	- The year-one pattern: sleep after the morning feed, again about five hours later in early afternoon, and overnight. Fenton: the transition "is something that almost all babies do. And it'll take about a year." **[unverified, unpublished]**
135	- **Mark Blumberg** (University of Iowa). "I've always been a terrible sleeper... we study the things that we're bad at." Never uses an alarm clock. **[solid, transcript]**
136	- Baby rats and baby humans "cycle very rapidly between sleep and wake... over the course of 24 hours, they can have hundreds of cycles." **[solid, transcript]**
137	- Dye tracing in newborn rats: the hypothalamic master clock has no wiring to brainstem sleep-wake centers at birth; a week later it does. "It's also happening in humans." **[solid, transcript]**
138	- "Prior to three to four months, there's very little you can do to help babies sleeping throughout the night. It's just gonna have to wait for the circadian system to connect them." **[solid; cf. Rivkees 2003, *Pediatrics* 112:373]**

140	- Lab: EEG caps on infants asleep in car seats — "the easiest experiment you can do"; "This baby's a champion twitcher." **[solid, transcript]**

142	- "A single twitch can produce activity in hundreds, probably thousands, of neurons... you're mapping your body." Blumberg, Marques and Iida 2013, *Curr Biol* 23:R532. **[solid]**
143	- Human follow-up: in 22 infants, twitches during quiet sleep rise sharply from ~3 months and are time-locked to sleep spindles. Sokoloff et al. 2021, *Curr Biol*. Lab page: "highlighted in Episode 5." https://blumberg.lab.uiowa.edu/node/41 **[solid]**
144	- **Rebecca Spencer** (UMass Amherst SomneuroLab). "I'm a lark"; postdoc at UC Berkeley in the mid-2000s when sleep-and-memory work took off. **[solid, transcript]**
145	- Infant study: 9-month-olds shown eight toys, four demonstrated with unusual actions; half nap, half are kept awake; the napper reproduces "three target objects," the non-napper "didn't remember any." **[solid, transcript; unpublished at filming]**
146	- Sleep spindles "happen simultaneously across the brain," moving memories from hippocampus to cortex; "in an infant, their hippocampus is smaller. So babies need to sleep in multiple sleep bouts, two naps and that overnight sleep." **[solid, transcript]**
147	- Landmark paper: Kurdziel, Duclos and Spencer 2013, *PNAS* 110:17267 — 40 preschoolers, ~78-minute classroom naps, ~10% more recall after napping, spindle density r = 0.65 with memory gain; only habitual nappers benefit. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3808582 **[solid]**
148	- Filmed March 2019 at UMass. https://www.massachusetts.edu/ada-exception-archive/umass-amherst-researcher-rebecca-spencer-featured-netflix-series-and-pbs-nova **[solid]**

243	- **Felix Warneken** (University of Michigan; formerly MPI Leipzig and Harvard). On camera he "clumsily knocks a cup off a table" and a toddler walks over to hand it back. https://michigantoday.umich.edu/2020/07/23/children-show-altruism-at-a-young-age **[solid]**
244	- Lit: Warneken and Tomasello 2006, *Science* 311:1301 — 24 eighteen-month-olds helped in 10 situations (out-of-reach objects, cabinets, wrong results); three human-raised chimpanzees helped only with reaching. **[solid; N via Michigan release]**
245	- MPG release: "virtually all children helped at least once," and 84% of helps came within 10 seconds, before eye contact. https://www.mpg.de/532681/pressRelease20060302 **[solid]**
246	- Rewards backfire: 20-month-olds given a toy for helping later helped less than those praised or given nothing. Warneken and Tomasello 2008, *Dev Psychol* 44:1785. **[solid]**
247	- **Laura Schulz** (MIT Early Childhood Cognition Lab): CBMM confirms the series "features CBMM PI Laura Schulz and her research with toddlers." **[appearance solid]**
248	- Most likely study: 15-month-olds who watch an adult struggle before succeeding try harder on a novel toy (N = 262 across three experiments). Leonard, Lee and Schulz 2017, *Science* 357:1290. **[study inferred]**
249	- Reviews mention toddlers understanding desires and "other people's minds and needs" (cf. Repacholi and Gopnik 1997, *Dev Psychol* 33:12 — 18-month-olds hand over the broccoli the adult prefers; 14-month-olds hand over crackers). **[solid lit; attribution unknown]**
250	- Third scientist: **unidentified**. **[unverified]**

254	## 2. Literature greatest hits, by theme
255	
256	### Sleep
257	- Newborns (0–2 months) sleep a mean 14.6 h/day (range 9.3–20.0); 3 months 13.6; 6 months 12.9; 12 months 12.9; 1–2 years 12.6. Galland et al. 2012, *Sleep Med Rev* (34 studies). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21784676/ **[solid]**
258	- Infants in predominantly Asian countries sleep about an hour less across childhood. Galland 2012. **[solid]**
259	- Half of newborn sleep is REM (about a third of the whole day); REM falls to ~20–25% by age 3; at 30 weeks' gestation it is ~80%. Roffwarg, Muzio and Dement 1966, *Science* 152:604. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.152.3722.604 **[solid]**
260	- Newborns fall asleep straight into REM: ~60% of sleep onsets at 3 weeks vs 20% at 6 months; adults enter via NREM. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9602694/ **[solid]**
261	- Sleep spindles appear at ~2 months; K-complexes by ~6 months (Jenni et al. 2004). **[solid]**
262	- Circadian rhythms switch on after ~2 months (Rivkees 2003, *Pediatrics* 112:373). **[solid]**
263	- Night wakings: 0–3.4 per night at 0–2 months, 0–2.5 at 1–2 years; the longest sleep stretch grows ~39 minutes per month in the first half-year. Galland 2012. **[solid]**
264	- "Sleeping through" is a minority skill: at 6 months 62.4% manage 6 unbroken hours and 43.0% manage 8; at 12 months 72.1% and 56.6%; no link to later development. Pennestri et al. 2018, *Pediatrics* 142:e20174330 (388 infants). **[solid]**
265	- Sleep regressions at 4/8/12 months: no peer-reviewed support for discrete universal regressions; app data from 841 children and 156,989 logged sessions show smooth consolidation. Mindell et al. 2016. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26987761/ **[pop]**
266	- Naps consolidate preschool memory by ~10%; spindle density predicts the gain (r = 0.65). Kurdziel, Duclos and Spencer 2013, *PNAS*. **[solid]**
267	- Sleep's job flips at ~2.4 years from neural reorganization (REM-heavy) to repair, in a model fit to 60+ datasets. Cao et al. 2020, *Sci Adv* 6:eaba0398. **[solid, model-based]**
268	- Blumberg's informal estimate: an infant's limbs twitch "at least 40,000 times a day." https://now.uiowa.edu/node/37661 **[informal estimate]**
269	- Sleep training in 43 infants: faster sleep onset, lower cortisol, no attachment or behavior differences at 12 months (Gradisar et al. 2016, *Pediatrics*); 5-year follow-up of 326 children found no harms and no benefits (Price et al. 2012, *Pediatrics*). **[solid, small samples]**
270	
271	### Crying
272	- Crying rises to a peak around 6 weeks: Brazelton 1962, *Pediatrics* 29:579 (80 diaries, ~2¼ h/day through week 7). **[solid]**
273	- Meta-analysis of 8,690 infants: 117–133 minutes/day of fuss/cry in weeks 1–6, ~68 minutes at 10–12 weeks; individual range 30 minutes to over 5 hours. Wolke, Bilgin and Samara 2017, *J Pediatr* 185:55. **[solid]**
274	- Colic by country: Denmark 5.5% and Germany 6.7% at 3–4 weeks; UK 28% at 1–2 weeks, Canada 34.1% at 3–4 weeks, Italy 20.9% at 8–9 weeks. Wolke 2017. **[solid]**
275	- Colic fades fast: 17–25% in weeks 1–6, 11% at 8–9 weeks, 0.6% at 10–12 weeks. Wolke 2017. **[solid]**
276	- Wessel's rule of threes (1954, *Pediatrics* 14:421): crying more than 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for 3 weeks; prevalence 1.5–40% depending on definition. **[definition solid; prevalence contested]**
277	- Shaken-baby hospitalizations track the crying curve, peaking at 10–13 weeks (273 California cases); basis of Barr's "Period of PURPLE Crying." Barr, Trent and Cross 2006, *Child Abuse Negl* 30:7. **[solid]**
278	- Newborns cry in their mother tongue: 30 French and 30 German 2–5-day-olds, 1,254 cries — French cries rise in pitch, German cries fall. Mampe et al. 2009, *Curr Biol* 19:1994. **[solid, single study]**
279	- Newborns do make tears: term newborns' basal tear production (Schirmer 9.2 mm) is adult-like; preterm 3.5 mm. Isenberg et al. 1998, *Arch Ophthalmol* 116:773; Toker 2002. The "no tears until 1–3 months" line is folklore. **[pop claim contradicted]**
280	- Contagious crying: newborns cry to another newborn's cry but not to a recording of their own. Martin and Clark 1982, *Dev Psychol* 18:3. **[solid]**
281	
282	### Feeding
283	- Day-one colostrum totals about 15 mL — three teaspoons: 1.5 ± 1.1 g per feed, 15 ± 11 g/day in 90 newborns. Santoro et al. 2010, *J Pediatr* 156:29. **[solid]**
284	- Newborn stomach capacity is ~20 mL; the viral cherry/walnut/egg poster traces to early-1900s data of undetermined accuracy. Bergman 2013, *Acta Paediatr* 102:773; Spangler et al. 2008, *J Hum Lact* 24:199. **[contested / pop]**
285	- Milk has a clock: melatonin undetectable by day, peaking near midnight (~47 pg/mL); cortisol peaks in the morning; fat peaks in the evening. Italianer et al. 2020, *Nutrients* 12:2328 (71 components). **[solid]**
286	- Milk from mothers of 31 febrile infants carried more leukocytes, macrophages and TNF-α than after recovery. Riskin et al. 2012, *Pediatr Res* 71:220. **[solid, small]**
287	- Taste at birth: sweet relaxes, sour purses, bitter gapes; salt is ignored until a preference switches on at ~4 months. Rosenstein and Oster 1988, *Child Dev* 59:1555; Beauchamp, Cowart and Moran 1986, *Dev Psychobiol* 19:17. **[solid]**
288	- "10,000 taste buds" is folklore; adult counts run ~2,000–8,000 (Miller and Reedy 1990, *Physiol Behav* 47:1213). **[contested]**
289	- Birth seeds the microbiome: vaginally born babies carry Lactobacillus and Prevotella like their mother's vagina; C-section babies carry Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium like skin. Dominguez-Bello et al. 2010, *PNAS* 107:11971 (10 newborns). **[solid, tiny n]**
290	- Vaginal seeding pilot: 18 infants, 4 swabbed with gauze incubated in the mother's vagina; partial restoration, no health outcomes. Dominguez-Bello et al. 2016, *Nat Med*. **[solid, pilot]**
291	- Baby Biome Study: Bacteroides abundant in 51% of vaginally born babies but low or absent in 99.6% of 282 C-section babies; C-section babies carried hospital Enterococcus and Klebsiella; differences largely gone by one year. Shao et al. 2019, *Nature* 574:117 (771 babies). **[solid]**
292	- Early peanut cuts allergy: 640 high-risk infants randomized at 4–11 months; allergy at 5 was 13.7% with avoidance vs 1.9% with consumption (86% relative reduction); 35.3% vs 10.6% in skin-test-positive infants. Du Toit et al. 2015, *NEJM* 372:803 (LEAP). **[solid]**
293	- Breastfeeding and IQ: 3,493 Brazilian adults — ≥12 months of breastfeeding predicted +3.76 IQ points and 341 reais/month more income at 30 (Victora et al. 2015, *Lancet Glob Health*); PROBIT's 17,046 Belarusian infants showed +7.5 verbal IQ at 6.5 years (Kramer 2008). **[contested]**
294	- Sibling comparisons erase 10 of 11 claimed breastfeeding benefits. Colen and Ramey 2014, *Soc Sci Med* 109:55. **[contested]**
295	- Skin-to-skin after birth makes breastfeeding at 1–4 months ~24% more likely (RR ≈ 1.24). Moore, Bergman, Anderson and Medley 2016, Cochrane CD003519. **[solid]**
296	
297	### Movement
298	- Learning to walk: 12–19-month-olds average 2,368 steps and 17 falls per hour of free play and travel 701 m — "7.7 American football fields" — per hour. Adolph et al. 2012, *Psychol Sci* 23:1387 (151 infants). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3591461/ **[solid]**
299	- The daily figures — ~14,000 steps, ~46 football fields, ~100 falls — are the authors' extrapolation (hourly rate × 6 waking hours). Same paper. **[solid as estimate]**
300	- Novice walkers travel farther and faster than expert crawlers with the same fall rate; efficiency without extra cost is why crawlers switch. Same paper. **[solid]**
301	- No transfer across postures: experienced 12-month crawlers never attempt a 90-cm cliff, but 10 of 16 (63%) 12-month novice walkers go over it. Kretch and Adolph 2013, *Child Dev* 84:226. **[solid]**
302	- Walkers attempt risky drop-offs 80% of the time at 3 cm beyond their ability; crawlers 10%. Same paper. **[solid]**
303	- WHO milestone windows (1st–99th percentile, months): sitting unsupported 3.8–9.2; hands-and-knees crawling 5.2–13.5; standing alone 6.9–16.9; walking alone 8.2–17.6. WHO MGRS 2006, *Acta Paediatr* Suppl 450:86 (816 children, 5 countries). **[solid]**
304	- 4.3% of children never crawl on hands and knees; ~90% hit five milestones in a common order. Same paper. **[solid]**
305	- Newborn stepping disappears by ~2–3 months because legs get heavy, not because the brain forgets: ankle weights abolish it, submerging the legs in water restores it. Thelen, Fisher and Ridley-Johnson 1984, *Infant Behav Dev* 7:479. **[solid]**
306	- 7-month-olds who show no stepping on the floor step on a moving treadmill. Thelen 1986, *Child Dev* 57:1498. **[solid]**
307	- Daily practice of the stepping reflex kept it going to 8 weeks and brought earlier walking. Zelazo, Zelazo and Kolb 1972, *Science* 176:314. **[solid; walking ages not retrieved]**
308	- Palmar grasp: Louis Robinson (1891) hung "upward of sixty" newborns from a stick; nearly all held ≥10 seconds, record 2 min 35 s by a 3-week-old. *Popular Science Monthly*, March 1892. **[solid as Victorian report]**
309	- Reflex exit dates (StatPearls): Moro by ~6 months; palmar grasp ~6 months; rooting fades after 1 month; stepping ~2–3 months; asymmetric tonic neck ~3–6 months; Babinski 12–24 months. **[solid ranges]**
310	- Pincer grasp: CDC lists "picks things up between thumb and pointer finger" at 12 months; clinical sources say 9–10 months. **[solid]**
311	- Back to Sleep did not delay walking: 351 infants; prone sleepers rolled, sat and crawled earlier but walked at the same age. Davis et al. 1998, *Pediatrics* 102:1135. **[solid]**
312	- SIDS fell more than 50% from 1994 to 2016 after Back to Sleep (NICHD). **[solid]**
313	- Culture: 64 rural Kenyan (Kipsigis) babies sat and walked early because adults deliberately trained them (Super 1976, *Dev Med Child Neurol* 18:561); Hopi cradleboards did not delay walking (Dennis and Dennis 1940). **[solid]**
314	- Baby walkers: each 24 hours in a walker delays walking ~3 days and standing ~4 days (Garrett 2002, *BMJ*); Canada banned them in April 2004, the first country to do so; US walker injuries fell from 21,000 (1990) to 3,200 (2003). **[solid]**
315	- Tummy time: 16 studies, 4,237 infants; modest gross-motor and flat-head benefits, almost all questionnaire-based. Hewitt et al. 2020, *Pediatrics* 145:e20192168. **[solid, weak base]**
316	
317	### Language
318	- Perceptual narrowing: 11 of 12 English-learning 6–8-month-olds discriminated Hindi retroflex/dental contrasts; 8 of 12 at 8–10 months; 2 of 10 at 10–12 months; only 3 of 10 English adults. Werker and Tees 1984, *Infant Behav Dev* 7:49. **[solid]**
319	- Longitudinally, all 6 infants passed at 6–8 months and none of the 6 at 10–12 months. Same paper. **[solid]**
320	- Perceptual magnet by 6 months: 32 Swedish and 32 American infants each treated their own language's vowel prototype as a magnet. Kuhl et al. 1992, *Science* 255:606. **[solid]**
321	- Social gating: 9-month-old Americans learned Mandarin contrasts from live tutors in 12 sessions (~5 hours; 65.7% vs 56.7%) but learned nothing from the same tutors on DVD or audio. Kuhl, Tsao and Liu 2003, *PNAS* 100:9096. **[solid]**
322	- Statistical learning: 8-month-olds segment words from 2 minutes of monotone nonsense. Saffran, Aslin and Newport 1996, *Science* 274:1926. **[solid]**
323	- Parentese pays: 11–14-month-olds who heard the most one-on-one parentese had 433 words at 24 months vs 169 for those who heard least. Ramírez-Esparza, García-Sierra and Kuhl 2014, *Dev Sci* 17:880. **[solid]**
324	- Coaching parents in parentese at 6, 10 and 14 months raised 18-month vocabulary (~100 vs ~60 words; d = 0.53). Ferjan Ramírez, Lytle and Kuhl 2020, *PNAS* 117:3484. **[solid]**
325	- The 30-million-word gap: Hart and Risley 1995 recorded 42 families one hour a month for 2.5 years; 2,153 vs 616 words per hour by SES, extrapolated to 45M vs 13M words by age 4. https://www.aft.org/ae/spring2003/hart_risley **[solid as reported]**
326	- Not reproduced: counting all caregivers and overheard speech erases much of the gap (Sperry, Sperry and Miller 2019, *Child Dev* 90:1303); LENA recordings of 329 families (49,765 hours) put the gap nearer 4 million words by age 4 (Gilkerson et al. 2017). **[contested]**
327	- Processing speed: by 24 months lower-SES toddlers were ~6 months behind in real-time word recognition. Fernald, Marchman and Weisleder 2013, *Dev Sci* 16:234. **[solid]**
328	- Baby videos: each daily hour of baby DVDs went with 6–8 fewer understood words at 8–16 months. Zimmerman, Christakis and Meltzoff 2007, *J Pediatr* 151:364. **[solid, correlational]**
329	- A month of Baby Einstein taught 12–18-month-olds no new words; parents who liked the DVD overestimated learning. DeLoache et al. 2010, *Psychol Sci* 21:1570. **[solid]**
330	- Disney dropped "educational" in 2006 after an FTC complaint and in October 2009 refunded $15.99 per DVD, up to four per household. https://www.washington.edu/news/2009/10/29/disney-offers-refunds-for-baby-einstein-products/ **[solid]**
331	- Milestones: canonical babbling ~6 months; first words ~8–14 months; ~50 words at 18 months and 200–300 at 24 months are standard CDI norms (Fenson et al. 1994). **[solid range; medians not re-verified]**
332	- The "vocabulary spurt" is rare: only 5 of 38 children fit a spurt curve better than steady acceleration. Ganger and Brent 2004, *Dev Psychol*. **[contested as universal stage]**
333	- Pointing emerges ~12 months and predicts later language (meta-analytic r = .52 concurrent; Colonnesi et al. 2010, *Dev Rev*); declarative pointing is the human-specific part (Tomasello, Carpenter and Liszkowski 2007, *Child Dev* 78:705). **[solid; effect size contested]**
334	- Bilingual 7-month-olds switch anticipatory looks when a rule changes; monolinguals don't (Kovács and Mehler 2009, *PNAS*); a 2023 multi-lab replication questions robustness. **[contested]**
335	- Newborns of Tagalog–English mothers prefer both languages equally and still tell them apart. Byers-Heinlein, Burns and Werker 2010, *Psychol Sci* 21:343. **[solid]**
336	- Baby sign language teaches signs, not language: 40 infants followed 8–20 months, no vocabulary advantage. Kirk et al. 2013, *Child Dev* 84:574. **[solid]**
337	- Fast mapping: preschoolers who heard "the chromium tray, not the red one" once remembered the color word a week later. Carey and Bartlett 1978. **[solid]**
338	- Vowels learned in utero: 80 newborns aged 7–75 hours in Sweden and the US sucked more for non-native vowels. Moon, Lagercrantz and Kuhl 2013, *Acta Paediatr* 102:156. **[solid]**
339	
340	### Cognition
341	- Drawbridge: 3.5–4.5-month-olds look longer when a screen rotates "through" a hidden box — object permanence long before Piaget's 8–12 months. Baillargeon 1987, *Dev Psychol* 23:655; Baillargeon, Spelke and Wasserman 1985, *Cognition* 20:191. **[solid]**
342	- Number: 6-month-olds tell 8 from 16 dots but not 8 from 12 (Xu and Spelke 2000, *Cognition* 74:B1); 9-month-olds manage 8 vs 12 (Lipton and Spelke 2003, *Psychol Sci*). **[solid]**
343	- Newborns 49 hours old match 4 vs 12 syllables to 4 vs 12 objects, 15 of 16 of them. Izard et al. 2009, *PNAS* 106:10382. **[solid]**
344	- Infant arithmetic: 5-month-olds look longer when 1 + 1 doll yields 1. Wynn 1992, *Nature* 358:749. **[solid]**
345	- Intuitive statistics: 8-month-olds look longer (9.9 s vs 7.5 s) when 4 red balls are drawn from a box of 70 white and 5 red — unless the balls come from the experimenter's pocket. Xu and Garcia 2008, *PNAS* 105:5012. **[solid]**
346	- 15-month-olds reason from samples: 80% vs 33% tried the other toy depending on which box the squeaky balls came from. Gweon, Tenenbaum and Schulz 2010, *PNAS* 107:9066. **[solid]**
347	- Goldilocks effect: 7–8-month-olds look away from events that are too predictable and from events that are too surprising, a U-shape in 72 infants. Kidd, Piantadosi and Aslin 2012, *PLoS ONE* 7:e36399. **[solid]**
348	- Little scientists: 110 eleven-month-olds who saw a ball pass through a wall then banged the ball; those who saw it float dropped it. Stahl and Feigenson 2015, *Science* 348:91. **[solid]**
349	- Fantz 1963: infants under 5 days old look longer at black-and-white patterns than plain color — the birth of the looking-time method. *Science* 140:296. **[solid]**
350	- Memory: 9-month-olds imitate after 24 hours, 14-month-olds after a week (Meltzoff 1988); adults' earliest memories date to ~3–3.5 years in a corpus of over 11,000 memories (Rubin 2000, *Memory* 8:265). **[solid]**
351	- 5–7-year-olds recall over 60% of events discussed at age 3; 8–9-year-olds under 40%. Bauer and Larkina 2014, *Memory* 22:907. **[solid]**
352	- Mirror self-recognition: ~65% at 20–24 months (Amsterdam 1972); but 2 of 82 Kenyan children, 0% in Fiji (Broesch et al. 2011) and 7% of ni-Vanuatu vs 68% of Canadian toddlers (Cebioğlu and Broesch 2021). **[solid; interpretation contested]**
353	- Neonatal imitation: Meltzoff and Moore 1977 (*Science*, 6 infants aged 12–21 days) vs 106 newborns tested at 1, 3, 6 and 9 weeks with 11 models who imitated nothing. Oostenbroek et al. 2016, *Curr Biol* 26:1334. **[contested, leaning debunked]**
354	- Cross-modal: 1-month-olds looked longer at the pacifier shape they had sucked unseen (Meltzoff and Borton 1979, *Nature* 282:403), later not replicated; shapes bias color preference in 2–3-month-olds but not 8-month-olds (Wagner and Dobkins 2011, *Psychol Sci* 22:1067). **[contested / solid]**
355	- Persistence is contagious: 15-month-olds who watched an adult struggle tried harder (Leonard, Lee and Schulz 2017, *Science*; N = 262). **[solid]**
356	- Marshmallow test: the effect on age-15 achievement is about half the original in a ~900-child replication, and most of it comes from waiting ≥20 seconds. Watts, Duncan and Quan 2018, *Psychol Sci*. **[contested original]**
357	- Perceptual narrowing for faces: 6-month-olds discriminate individual monkey faces; 9-month-olds and adults cannot. Pascalis, de Haan and Nelson 2002, *Science* 296:1321. **[solid]**
358	- Blicket detector: 2–4-year-olds categorize objects by a novel causal power. Gopnik and Sobel 2000, *Child Dev* 71:1205. **[solid]**
359

361	- Oxytocin: 80 couples, fathers' levels equal to mothers' (Gordon et al. 2010); gay primary-caregiving fathers' amygdalae respond like mothers' (Abraham et al. 2014, *PNAS*, 89 parents). **[solid]**
362	- Fathers' testosterone drops: 624 Filipino men followed 4.5 years; new fathers' morning T fell 26% and evening T 34% (vs 12%/14% in non-fathers); ≥3 hours of daily childcare predicted the lowest levels. Gettler et al. 2011, *PNAS* 108:16194. **[solid]**
363	- Mothers' brains remodel: gray-matter loss in social-cognition regions lasting ≥2 years, enough to classify every woman as pregnant or not (25 mothers vs 20 controls); no change in fathers. Hoekzema et al. 2017, *Nat Neurosci*. **[solid]**
364	- Still face: three phases (play, ~2 minutes of blank face, reunion); the YouTube demo has over 6 million views. **[solid]**
365	- The popular "matched only ~30% of the time, mismatches repaired in seconds" is Tronick's own summary of Tronick and Cohn 1989 (54 dyads), not a figure in a primary abstract. **[contested number]**
366	- Harlow's rhesus infants spent ~17–18 h/day on the cloth mother and under an hour on the wire mother that fed them. Harlow and Zimmermann 1959, *Science* 130:421. **[solid; hours via secondary]**
367	- Strange Situation: 8 episodes of ~3 minutes, ~21 minutes total, at 12–18 months. Ainsworth, Blehar, Waters and Wall 1978. **[solid]**
368	- Cross-cultural meta-analysis of 32 samples (~1,990 infants): 65% secure, 21% avoidant, 14% resistant; within-country variation exceeds between-country. van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg 1988, *Child Dev*. **[solid]**
369	- Disorganized attachment ~15% in low-risk samples, 48% in maltreated children. van IJzendoorn, Schuengel and Bakermans-Kranenburg 1999. **[solid]**
370	- Social smile ~2 months, chuckle ~4 months, laugh ~6 months (CDC milestones); stranger and separation wariness ~8–9 months. **[solid]**
371	- Social referencing: at a 30-cm visual-cliff drop, 74% of 12-month-olds crossed when mother smiled and none when she looked afraid. Sorce, Emde, Campos and Klinnert 1985, *Dev Psychol* 21:195. **[solid]**
372	- Eye contact: 2–5-day-olds looked 106.8 s at direct-gaze faces vs 63.7 s at averted gaze (17 newborns). Farroni et al. 2002, *PNAS* 99:9602. **[solid]**
373	- Helping: 18-month-olds help within seconds, before eye contact (Warneken and Tomasello 2006); a toy reward makes 20-month-olds help less (2008). **[solid]**
374	- Fairness: 15-month-olds look longer at an unequal cracker split (10.57 s vs 8.07 s); the ones who share their favorite toy are the ones most bothered by unfairness. Schmidt and Sommerville 2011, *PLoS ONE* 6:e23223. **[solid]**
375	- 19-month-olds expect two giraffes to get one toy each; 21-month-olds expect reward to go only to the one who worked. Sloane, Baillargeon and Premack 2012, *Psychol Sci*. **[solid]**
376	- In-group taste: after choosing a food, 87.5% of infants chose the puppet who liked the same food (single-trial design). Mahajan and Wynn 2012, *Cognition* 124:227. **[contested]**
377	- Helper/hinderer: ManyBabies 4 (567 infants, 37 labs) found 49.3% helper choice. **[contested]**
378	- Bucharest Early Intervention Project: 136 institutionalized toddlers randomized to foster care or care-as-usual; foster-care children had higher cognitive scores at 42 and 54 months, most for those placed before ~24 months. Nelson et al. 2007, *Science* 318:1937. **[solid]**
379	- At age 8, BEIP IQ was 81.5 (foster) vs 76.2 (institution), p = .07; children placed before 26 months fared best. Fox et al. 2011, *JCPP*. **[solid]**
380	- Kangaroo care: immediate skin-to-skin for 3,211 infants weighing 1.0–1.8 kg cut 28-day mortality from 15.7% to 12.0% (RR 0.75); 16.9 vs 1.5 h/day of contact; trial stopped early. WHO iKMC 2021, *NEJM* 384:2028. **[solid]**
381	- Twenty years on, Colombian kangaroo-care babies had less school absence and aggression and a larger left caudate (264 analysed). Charpak et al. 2017, *Pediatrics* 139:e20162063. **[solid]**
382	- Aka fathers (Central Africa) hold infants 22% of in-camp time and are within arm's reach 51.5% of the day — "at least five times more than fathers in any other human population" (Hewlett). **[solid]**
383	- Co-sleeping: 25% of US families always or almost always bed-shared and 42% sometimes (NCHS 1991–99); 93% in an Indian sample (Bharti 2006). **[solid; global % contested]**
384	- Parallel play is typical from ~24–30 months (Parten 1932). **[solid textbook]**
385	- Mothers of 11-month-old girls underestimated, mothers of boys overestimated, their babies' crawling on slopes; actual performance was identical. Mondschein, Adolph and Tamis-LeMonda 2000, *J Exp Child Psychol* 77:304. **[solid]**
386	- Temperament: ~20% of 4-month-olds are "high-reactive," four times more likely to be inhibited at 4 and about half anxious by 7 (Kagan and Snidman 2004). **[solid; 20–25%]**
387	- Thomas and Chess's NYLS (141 children): 40% easy, 10% difficult, 15% slow-to-warm. **[solid]**
388	- Heritability of infant temperament ~.20–.60 in twin studies (Saudino 2005). **[solid]**
389	- Rat pups licked and groomed more have less methylation at the hippocampal glucocorticoid-receptor gene and calmer stress responses; reversed by cross-fostering (Weaver et al. 2004, *Nat Neurosci* 7:847). Human extrapolation is a leap. **[solid in rats]**
390	- Dunedin: self-control at ages 3–11 in 1,037 children predicted adult outcomes at 32 — criminal conviction 13% vs 43%, income under NZ$20k 10% vs 32% for top vs bottom fifth. Moffitt et al. 2011, *PNAS* 108:2693. **[solid]**
391	- Birth order has essentially no effect on personality in 20,000 people. Rohrer, Egloff and Schmukle 2015, *PNAS*. **[solid]**
392	
393	### Senses
394	- Newborn vision: acuity ~1 cycle/degree, roughly 20/400–20/800; adult-like by ~3–5 years. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9314692/ **[solid; Snellen conversion contested]**
395	- Fixed focus: alert newborns focus best at a median 19 cm (~7.5 inches); accommodation "approximates adult performance by the 4th month." Haynes, White and Held 1965, *Science* 148:528. **[solid]**
396	- Not colorblind: over 75% of neonates orient to a large saturated red patch; over 80% ignore blue; trichromatic by ~3 months. Adams et al. 1994; Teller 1998. **[solid]**
397	- Faces at 9 minutes old: 40 newborns (median age 9 min) tracked a face-like pattern farther than a scrambled one (Goren, Sarty and Wu 1975, *Pediatrics* 56:544; replicated by Johnson et al. 1991; failed by Easterbrook 1999). **[contested]**
398	- Mother's face within a day or two: newborns looked longer at mother than a stranger even with odor controlled. Bushnell, Sai and Mullin 1989, *Br J Dev Psychol* 7:3. **[solid]**
399	- Hearing: first fetal response at 19 weeks (500 Hz); by 27 weeks 96% respond to 250–500 Hz but none to 1,000–3,000 Hz; all respond to 3,000 Hz by 35 weeks. Hepper and Shahidullah 1994, *Arch Dis Child* 71:F81. **[solid]**
400	- Mother's voice: 8 of 10 newborns under 3 days old changed their sucking to hear mother rather than a stranger. DeCasper and Fifer 1980, *Science* 208:1174. **[solid]**
401	- Newborns prefer a passage read aloud daily in the last 6 weeks of pregnancy, even in a stranger's voice. DeCasper and Spence 1986, *Infant Behav Dev* 9:133. **[solid]**
402	- Smell: 22 of 30 newborns chose the unwashed breast (Varendi, Porter and Winberg 1994, *Lancet* 344:989); a breast-odor pad 17 cm away makes prone newborns crawl toward it (Varendi and Porter 2001). **[solid]**
403	- Pain: newborns' brains activate 18 of 20 adult pain regions, and a 128-mN poke in a newborn looks like a 512-mN poke in an adult (10 infants, 10 adults). Goksan et al. 2015, *eLife* 4:e06356. **[solid]**
404	- Until the mid-1980s newborns were sometimes operated on with muscle relaxants only; fentanyl blunted the stress response in preterm surgery. Anand and Hickey 1987, *NEJM* 317:1321. **[solid]**
405	- Head and body: a newborn's head is about a quarter of body length vs about an eighth in adults (textbook); Barbu-Roth's on-air "one third of the weight" is not a standard figure. **[solid / pop]**
406	
407	### Growth
408	- Saltatory growth: bursts of 0.5–2.5 cm separated by 2–63 days of nothing; 90–95% of infancy is growth-free (Lampl, Veldhuis and Johnson 1992, *Science*). **[solid, contested]**
409	- Weight doubles by ~4–6 months and triples by 12; length grows ~50% in year one (~50 to ~75 cm). **[solid textbook]**
410	- Brain volume +101% in year one and +15% in year two; gray matter +149%, cerebellum +240% in year one; ~83% of adult volume by age 2 (98 children). Knickmeyer et al. 2008, *J Neurosci* 28:12176. **[solid]**
411	- "One million new neural connections per second" (Harvard Center on the Developing Child) is uncited; earlier versions said 700–1,000; the order of magnitude is plausible but not measured. **[pop]**
412	- Measured synapses: ~2,500 per neuron at birth, peaking 50–60% above adult density; density peaks at ~3 months in auditory cortex and after 15 months in prefrontal cortex, then is pruned. Huttenlocher and Dabholkar 1997, *J Comp Neurol* 387:167. **[solid]**
413	- "300 bones fuse to 206": repeated everywhere, no primary source; the count depends on how cartilaginous elements and ossification centers are tallied. **[pop]**
414	- Fontanelles: six at birth; the anterior averages 2.1 cm and closes at a median 13.8 months; the posterior closes by ~2 months. Kiesler and Ricer 2003, *Am Fam Physician* 67:2547. **[solid]**
415	- Teething does not cause fever: 16 studies, 3,506 children; 70.5% show some sign (gum irritation 86.8%, irritability 68.2%, drooling 55.7%); temperature rises at most to 37.8 °C. Massignan et al. 2016, *Pediatrics* 137:e20153501. First tooth ~6 months. **[solid]**
416	
417	### Myths and busted claims (jokes live here)
418	- **Wonder Weeks**: ten "leaps" on a fixed calendar. Groningen PhD student Carolina de Weerth, with Paul van Geert, tested the schedule in 4 infants and found nothing (1998). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wonder_Weeks **[pop / contested]**
419	- De Weerth said Frans Plooij pressured her not to publish; the university let Plooij go in January 1998 (Volkskrant, 14 Jan 1998). Later studies: 28 infants, no pattern; 18 infants, fussiness only by maternal report. **[contested]**
420	- **Mozart effect**: 36 college students, a spatial-reasoning bump lasting ~10–15 minutes (Rauscher, Shaw and Ky 1993, *Nature*); never tested on babies; a 39-study meta-analysis found effects three times larger in Rauscher-affiliated labs and "little evidence left" (Pietschnig et al. 2010, *Intelligence* 38:314). **[debunked]**
421	- Georgia Governor Zell Miller budgeted $105,000 in 1998 to send every newborn home with a classical CD. **[solid]**
422	- **Baby Einstein**: see Language; refunds of $15.99 per DVD in October 2009. **[solid]**
423	- **30-million-word gap**: 42 families, hour-a-month samples, big extrapolation; not replicated as stated. **[contested]**
424	- **Neonatal imitation**: 106 newborns, 11 gestures, nothing. **[contested, leaning debunked]**
425	- **"Babies don't feel pain"**: surgery without anesthesia into the 1980s; fMRI says otherwise. **[debunked]**
426	- **Teething fever**: max 37.8 °C. **[debunked]**
427	- **Sleep regressions on a schedule**: no peer-reviewed support. **[pop]**
428	- **"Babies see upside down"**: every retina inverts the image at every age; a garbled Stratton 1896 inverting-goggles story. **[pop]**
429	- **Full-moon births**: 564,039 North Carolina births over 62 lunar cycles, no effect on birth frequency or complications. Arliss, Kaplan and Galvin 2005, *AJOG* 192:1462. **[debunked]**
430	- **Vaccines–autism**: Wakefield 1998, 12 children; 10 of 12 co-authors retracted the interpretation in 2004; paper retracted February 2010; Wakefield struck off 24 May 2010. **[debunked]**
431	- **Pacifiers and SIDS**: adjusted odds ratio 0.08 (185 cases, 312 controls; Li et al. 2006, *BMJ* 332:18) — press rounded to "90%"; association only. **[solid, correlational]**
432	- **Breast milk and IQ**: see Feeding. **[contested]**
433	- **Baby walkers help walking**: they delay it; Canada banned them. **[debunked]**
434	
435	---
436	
437	## 3. Hooks: 30 quotable, numeric, surprising lines (each with a source)
438	
439	1. A toddler takes about 2,368 steps and falls 17 times an hour — roughly 14,000 steps and 100 falls a day. Adolph et al. 2012, *Psychol Sci*. **[solid; daily figures extrapolated]**
440	2. Babies grow up to 2.5 cm overnight, then nothing for up to 63 days; 90–95% of infancy is growth-free. Lampl 1992, *Science*. **[solid, contested]**
441	3. On air: 62.7 cm one day, 64.5 the next — Lampl's first thought was "I'm really terrible at this." Netflix *Babies* Ep 3. **[solid]**
442	4. The growth-chart curve is connect-the-dots from 882 children measured monthly. Netflix *Babies* Ep 3. **[solid]**
443	5. Fathers' oxytocin matched mothers' in 80 couples; "Fatherhood is biological. It's as deep as motherhood." Gordon et al. 2010; Ep 1. **[solid]**
444	6. Gay dads raising babies from day one show mother-like amygdala activation; "It's a choice to be a parent to that infant." Abraham et al. 2014, *PNAS*; Ep 1. **[solid]**
445	7. Eight-month-olds learn made-up words like "pabeecoo" after two minutes of hearing them 45 times each. Saffran 1996, *Science*; Ep 4. **[solid]**
446	8. Only three bird groups and five mammal groups can learn new sounds: hummingbirds, parrots, songbirds, elephants, bats, dolphins, seals, humans. Jarvis 2019, *Science*; Ep 4. **[solid]**
447	9. Humans carry an extra copy of SRGAP2 that keeps neurons wired together longer, duplicated ~3.4, 2.4 and 1 million years ago. Dennis et al. 2012, *Cell*; Ep 4. **[solid]**
448	10. Six million logged events from ~1,000 babies: 1.5M sleeps, 2.5M feeds, 1.5M diapers — random at one month, a rhythm by one year. NYU Baby Sleep Study, Ep 5. **[unpublished]**
449	11. A sleeping baby's twitch is a sonar ping: one twitch fires "hundreds, probably thousands, of neurons" to map the body. Blumberg, Ep 5; Blumberg 2013, *Curr Biol*. **[solid]**
450	12. Babies cycle sleep and wake "hundreds" of times a day because the hypothalamic clock isn't wired to the brainstem yet; nothing fixes it before 3–4 months. Blumberg, Ep 5. **[solid]**
451	13. Half of a newborn's sleep is REM; adults get about 20%; at 30 weeks' gestation it's 80%. Roffwarg 1966, *Science*. **[solid]**
452	14. Only 43% of 6-month-olds sleep eight hours straight; at a year, 57%. Pennestri 2018, *Pediatrics*. **[solid]**
453	15. Newborn stepping uses two muscle patterns; toddlers add two more; rats, cats, macaques and guineafowl share them. Dominici 2011, *Science*; Ep 6. **[solid]**
454	16. Cowgill carried 130 pounds of gear through 15 museums to X-ray 600 children's bones, back to 250,000 years ago; Reviewer 2 said "Children's bones don't respond to exercise." Ep 6. **[solid]**
455	17. Toddler femurs are wide ovals, adult femurs upside-down teardrops, because toddlers waddle. Cowgill et al. 2010, *AJPA*. **[solid]**
456	18. Walkers have bigger vocabularies than same-age crawlers — and hear exactly the same number of words. Walle and Campos 2014; Ep 6. **[solid, parent-report]**
457	19. One five-minute block of a zoo day: 374 adult words. LENA recording, Ep 6. **[solid]**
458	20. French newborns cry with rising melody, German newborns with falling melody — 1,254 cries, 60 babies. Mampe 2009, *Curr Biol*. **[solid]**
459	21. Crying peaks around six weeks at ~2 hours a day; Danish babies cry least, British and Canadian most. Wolke 2017, *J Pediatr*. **[solid]**
460	22. Day-one colostrum: 1.5 grams a feed, 15 grams a day — three teaspoons. Santoro 2010, *J Pediatr*. **[solid]**
461	23. Milk leukocytes jump from 2% to as high as 94% when the baby gets sick. Hassiotou 2013. **[solid, small n]**
462	24. Rhesus mothers give sons richer milk and daughters more of it; 1.49 million Holsteins give ~445 kg more milk after a daughter. Hinde 2009; Hinde 2014. **[solid]**
463	25. Six-month-olds can tell 8 dots from 16 but not 8 from 12; two-day-olds match 4 vs 12 syllables to 4 vs 12 objects. Xu and Spelke 2000; Izard 2009. **[solid]**
464	26. Eleven-month-olds who watch a ball pass through a wall then bang the ball on the table; if it floated, they drop it. Stahl and Feigenson 2015, *Science*. **[solid]**
465	27. Six-month-olds can tell monkey faces apart; by nine months, like adults, they can't. Pascalis 2002, *Science*; Kang Lee, Ep 7. **[solid]**
466	28. Saxe scanned her own awake infant son and found face and scene regions "in the same place" as adults'. Deen 2017, *Nat Commun*; Ep 7. **[solid]**
467	29. The helper-vs-hinderer puppet show that launched infant morality: 567 babies in 37 labs later chose the helper 49.3% of the time. Hamlin 2007, *Nature*; ManyBabies 4, 2025. **[contested]**
468	30. The Wonder Weeks' ten leaps were tested on four babies by a PhD student who found nothing; her co-supervisor's co-author lost his job. de Weerth and van Geert 1998. **[pop]**
469	
470	Bonus lines: a newborn focuses at 19 cm, orients to red but not blue, and 22 of 30 pick the unwashed breast by smell (Haynes 1965; Adams 1994; Varendi 1994). Pointing starts at 12 months; mirror self-recognition at ~20–24 months in Western toddlers but 7% in Vanuatu (Amsterdam 1972; Cebioğlu and Broesch 2021). New fathers' testosterone drops 26–34% (Gettler 2011). Newborns were operated on without anesthesia until the mid-1980s (Anand and Hickey 1987).
471	
472	---
473	
474	## 4. Could not verify (do not sing these as fact)
475	
476	- Rosters for Ep 8 "Movement" (all three scientists), the touch and vision scientists in Ep 9 "Senses," and the third scientist in Eps 11 and 12. IMDb full credits returned 403; no press release, review or lab page named them.
477	- Which Part 2 episode holds Rebecca Saxe's segment (Ep 7 is most plausible); whether Mennella and Reddy are in Eps 9 and 10 respectively (inferred from topic).
478	- Rifkin-Graboi's 20-baby hippocampus result as a published paper; Fenton and Wallisch's app-data analysis (explicitly unpublished on air); Spencer's infant nap study as published.
479	- Georgieff's "shift the world's IQ by ten points"; Feldman's "a quarter" and "forever" amygdala lines; Barbu-Roth's "one third of body weight" head; Fenton's "16 hours" — all on-air glosses.
480	- Hamlin 2007 exact counts (often quoted as 14 of 16 and 12 of 12); Tronick's "30% matched" as a primary figure; Harlow's 17–18 hours as a primary figure; BEIP's "8–10 IQ points" at 54 months; "25 crawling variants"; Fenson CDI medians; the Rovee-Collier memory ladder (1 week at 3 months, 2 weeks at 6 months).
481	- Anne Fernald's appearance (a fan quotes page lists her in "First Words"; the episode audio does not include her).
482	- Kuhl, Dominguez-Bello, Charles Nelson, Spelke, Fei Xu, Tomasello, Fessler and Kidd appearing anywhere in the series.
